boundary_rationale: The stanza sequence opens the chapter with אֵיכָה֙ (oshb:Lam.4.1, byte tier), the aleph-line cry that also opens the poems at 1:1 and 2:1 (accent_stripped tier; sweep: 4 hits book-wide, verse-initial in three of them); WEB renders the cry “How the gold has become dim!” (web:Lam.4.1). Two verses of tarnished-treasure imagery, the gold and the sons of Zion counted as pitchers, give way to the narrator's indictment that “the daughter of my people has become cruel” (web:Lam.4.3), her cruelty toward her young set against nursing jackals — the verse's own doubled ketiv/qere pair disclosed here: unpointed ketiv תנין against pointed qere תַּנִּים֙ for the jackals themselves, and unpointed ketiv כי ענים against pointed qere כַּיְעֵנִ֖ים for the ostrich comparison (oshb:Lam.4.3, both notes single-witness apparatus), the plural nursing-jackals wording here following the qere rather than the singular ketiv — then pressed further by the Sodom comparison that closes the group: “the iniquity of the daughter of my people is greater than the sin of Sodom” (web:Lam.4.6). The stanzas run aleph, bet, gimel, dalet, he and vav, positions one through six of the reversed pe-before-ayin sequence that governs this chapter.

boundary_rationale: The poem's close turns to direct address: “Rejoice and be glad, daughter of Edom” (web:Lam.4.21) names בַּת אֱד֔וֹם directly (oshb:Lam.4.21, byte tier), the vocative opening the verse's warning about the cup that will pass to her. The close verse turns the same address back toward Zion and Edom together: בַּת צִיּ֔וֹן and בַּת אֱד֔וֹם both stand in 4:22 (oshb:Lam.4.22, byte tier) — “He will visit your iniquity, daughter of Edom.” (web:Lam.4.22). The stanzas run shin and tav, the closing two letters of the chapter's acrostic.

boundary_rationale: The fifth poem opens without an acrostic but with a three-imperative chain: זְכֹ֤ר יְהוָה֙ (oshb:Lam.5.1, byte tier) is followed in the same verse by a ketiv-qere pair, הביט הַבִּ֖יטָה (oshb:Lam.5.1, byte tier; the inventory's own K/Q note here), both readings meaning look or regard, and then by a third imperative carrying its own vav prefix, וּרְאֵ֥ה (oshb:Lam.5.1, byte tier); WEB renders the opening “Remember, Yahweh, what has come on us. Look, and see our reproach.” (web:Lam.5.1). As a petition imperative to the divine name, the remember-form stands in 2 verses, here and at web:Lam.3.19 (skeleton tier), the third member of its 3-verse bare-token census being the negated third-person perfect at web:Lam.2.1; the look-form stands in 2 verses as a bare token and in 4 under the single-letter prefix test, at web:Lam.1.11, web:Lam.2.20, web:Lam.3.63 and web:Lam.5.1 (skeleton tier at both digits). The communal voice then catalogs loss across 5:2-5:10 without a further direct address to YHWH: inheritance surrendered, “We are orphans and fatherless. Our mothers are as widows.” (web:Lam.5.3), water and wood bought at a price, foreign servitude, inherited guilt, and at the group's own close, the first-plural suffix עוֹרֵ֨נוּ֙ (oshb:Lam.5.10, byte tier), “Our skin is black like an oven, because of the burning heat of famine.” (web:Lam.5.10) — the catalogue's last first-plural form, standing immediately in front of a run of third-plural verbs on bare plural human-group subjects that opens at 5:11 and carries no first-plural form of its own.

boundary_rationale: This group opens on its own texture rather than continuing what precedes it: 5:11 through 5:14 each open with a bare plural human-group noun followed by a third-plural verb — נָשִׁים֙ (oshb:Lam.5.11, byte tier), “They ravished the women in Zion, the virgins in the cities of Judah.” (web:Lam.5.11); שָׂרִים֙ (oshb:Lam.5.12, byte tier); בַּחוּרִים֙ (oshb:Lam.5.13, byte tier); and זְקֵנִים֙ (oshb:Lam.5.14, byte tier) — none of the four carrying a first-plural form, against the first-plural catalogue that runs unbroken through the verse immediately in front of this span, web:Lam.5.10. The catalog continues from economic loss into social and personal violation: “The young men carry millstones. The children stumbled under loads of wood.” (web:Lam.5.13), princes hanged, elders gone from the gate. The group turns from external causes to the community's own confession, נָֽפְלָה֙ עֲטֶ֣רֶת — the crown fallen (oshb:Lam.5.16, byte tier) — “The crown has fallen from our head.” (web:Lam.5.16), the sixth of this span's eight verses. It closes on the desolation named directly, הַר צִיּוֹן֙ (oshb:Lam.5.18, byte tier), “the mountain of Zion, which is desolate” (web:Lam.5.18); the verse also carries this poem's only parashah mark, tier-3 weak and single-witness (the PE type marks 1 verse here; the samekh type marks 0 verses in this poem, the two never conflated), corroborating a close already carried by the discourse turn to direct address that follows at web:Lam.5.19 rather than driving it.
